title: Val's in Cleveland, Lannie Scott, and Tatum as harmonic pioneer
summary: Wilson describes Val's upright piano and Lannie Scott, and argues that Tatum invented the harmonic approach that later players took for granted.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Because Val's was the place. Val's had that big old upright piano in there, and Art loved it. Every time he was in Cleveland, and all the piano players from miles around would come when they heard Art come to town, and one of the fellows who I believe got on to Art first and started catching on to the key of those harmonic before any of us records of Art was Lannie Scott.
Yes, Lannie Scott in Cleveland began to understand a little bit of what Art was doing, because Art was a real pioneer -- no one was even thinking of notes like Art did in those days.
So much of it was just like out of the blue sky, where you could trace some roots in Fats and Earl, going back through the history of great players --

Uh huh. So much of it began with Art, as far as I could tell, anyway. Of course he was a great stride player, because we could trace stride back to much older players, since stride had been mastered by James P. Johnson by the First World War, as James P. Johnson was just fantastic with that stride.
But that harmonic thing, why, no one was even
thinking in those terms, that's common with young players today. But in those days, Tatum invented that whole thing as far as I am able to ascertain.
